questions.q: What does a missing value look like inside a Pandas DataFrame?
options: NaN (Not a Number) — Pandas' explicit marker for 'no value was here,' regardless of column type
The text 'NULL' as a literal string
The number zero
An empty string, always
questions.explain: NaN is Pandas' universal marker for missing data, distinct from an empty string or a zero — it explicitly means no value was recorded.

options: A new DataFrame with missing values already removed
A count of total rows in the DataFrame
The actual missing values themselves
True/False for every cell, with True marking exactly where values are missing
questions.explain: .isna() produces a same-shaped DataFrame of True/False values, letting you see exactly which cells are missing before deciding what to do.

questions.q: What does .isna().sum() give you that .isna() alone doesn't?
options: A per-column count of how many missing values exist, rather than a True/False grid
Nothing different — they return identical output
The average of all non-missing values
The exact row numbers of missing values
questions.explain: Summing the True/False grid (True counts as 1) collapses it into a quick per-column total, a fast way to gauge how bad the gaps are.

questions.q: What is the key consideration before using .fillna(0) on a revenue column?
options: .fillna(0) should always be used on every numeric column automatically
Whether a missing value actually means 'zero sales' or means 'we don't know' — those are very different things to report on
Whether the DataFrame has more than 1000 rows
Whether the column contains any negative numbers
questions.explain: Filling missing data requires understanding what the gap actually represents — treating 'unknown' as 'zero' can silently distort real analysis.

questions.q: When is .dropna() the right choice instead of .fillna()?
options: Never — dropna() should be avoided in all cases
When a missing value makes the row genuinely unusable, rather than having a sensible default to fill it with
Always — dropna() is universally more correct than fillna()
Only when the DataFrame has no missing values at all
questions.explain: The right tool depends on what the missing value means: dropna() when the row can't be sensibly completed, fillna() when a reasonable default genuinely exists.
